# An attained hinge potential for covers of every mixed-integer fiber

This note supplies a new variational object and its exact necessary
conditions. It does not establish the OC cap budget. In particular, the
joint first-order system below can have a zero objective multiplier.

Fix a finite nonempty set `P subset Z^n`, with `n>=1,d>=1`, and convex
bodies `K_z subset R^d` for `z in P`. Put

`S=union_z ({z} x K_z)`, `mu=sum_z vol_d|K_z`, `M=mu(S)>0`.

The fibers need not be compatible for the compactness theorem. In its
intended application they are the positive fibers of one convex body.
Every fiber in this note has positive `d`-volume. Zero-volume fibers and
intrinsic lower-dimensional measures are outside this lemma's scope.

For a fixed positive integer `N`, consider affine functions

`L_i(z,x)=a_i dot z+u_i dot x-b_i`, `|u_i|=1`, `i=1,...,N`.

Their caps are the CLOSED ambient halfspaces `H_i={L_i>=0}`. Integer
normals `a_i` are arbitrary real vectors and may be unbounded across a
sequence. Thus oblique cuts are retained. Given `0<tau<1`, impose

`S subset union_i H_i`, and `mu(H_i)<=tau M` for every `i`.       (1)

Define the continuously normalized hinge potential

`Psi(L)=sum_i integral_S (L_i)_+ dmu`.                           (2)

The normalization is in the continuous coordinates, not in the full
ambient space. Multiplying a halfspace's defining function by a positive
constant and then restoring `|u_i|=1` leaves (2) unchanged.

## 1. Attainment at fixed cap count and budget

If (1) is feasible, (2) attains a finite minimum among all such `N`-cap
families. That minimum is strictly positive.

Proof. Choose a minimizing sequence with total potential bounded by a
fixed finite `B`. For each `i,z` write

`t_iz=b_i-a_i dot z`.

Choose `R` with every `K_z subset R B_d`, and write `m_z=|K_z|>0`.
The contribution from fiber `z` to cap `i` is at least
`m_z(-R-t_iz)_+`. Hence

`t_iz>=-R-B/m_z`.                                               (3)

After taking a subsequence, all `u_i` converge to unit vectors and each
of the finitely many thresholds `t_iz` converges either to a finite real
number or to `+infinity`. A threshold cannot tend to negative infinity
by (3).

For completeness, the required exact realization of these limiting
traces is as follows. Let

`E={ (b-a dot z)_(z in P): a in R^n,b in R } subset R^P`.

Fix one cap, let `I` be its finite-threshold coordinates, and `J` the
remaining coordinates. The restriction image `E|I` is a finite-dimensional
linear subspace and is closed. Thus there is `v in E` agreeing with all
finite limiting thresholds. Choose a linear right inverse `R_I` of the
restriction map onto its image. If `e_k` is the approximating trace,
the exact vectors

`h_k=e_k-v-R_I(e_k|I-v|I)`

belong to `ker(E -> R^I)`, and their `J` coordinates tend to
`+infinity`. One sufficiently late member `h` has all its `J`
coordinates strictly positive. Therefore `v+T h`, for sufficiently large
finite `T`, still equals every required finite threshold and is greater
than `R` on every coordinate in `J`. It belongs to `E` and is realized
by finite `a,b`. If `I` or `J` is empty the same argument uses the zero
restriction map or omits the unnecessary saturation, respectively.

Perform this construction independently for every cap. On finite-trace
fibers the hinges converge uniformly, because the normals and thresholds
converge. On an infinite-trace fiber the hinge is eventually identically
zero and its realized limiting cap is empty. Consequently (2) converges
exactly to the potential of the realized finite family.

Cap masses converge as well. On each finite-trace fiber the limiting
boundary is a genuine continuous hyperplane (`|u_i|=1`), of zero
`d`-volume. Dominated convergence applies to the cap indicators.
On infinite-trace fibers the cap is empty. Thus all the budget bounds
in (1) survive, including their exact constants.

Coverage survives pointwise. Fix `(z,x) in S`. Some cap contains this
point along infinitely many members of the sequence, since there are
only `N` caps. Its threshold on `z` cannot diverge to infinity, and its
limiting margin is nonnegative. The saturation leaves that finite margin
unchanged. Hence at least one realized CLOSED cap still contains the
point. This proves attainment and preserves all boundary points.

There is also an explicit positive lower bound. Let `r_z>0` be any
inball radius of `K_z`, and let `kappa_(d-1)` denote the volume of the
unit ball in `R^(d-1)` (with `kappa_0=1`). A cap containing the center of
this inball has hinge integral over that ball at least

`integral_(r_z B_d) (u dot x)_+ dx
   =kappa_(d-1) r_z^(d+1)/(d+1)`.

The identity follows by integrating
`t kappa_(d-1)(r_z^2-t^2)^((d-1)/2)` from `0` to `r_z`.
Choose one covering cap at each inball center and sum its own-fiber
contribution. Every such contribution is part of (2), so

`Psi >= kappa_(d-1)/(d+1) * sum_z r_z^(d+1)>0`.                 (4)

This is a geometric lower bound on the new potential, not a lower bound
on the required cap budget. QED.

## 2. Why ambient normalization does not have this property

Consider `C=[0,1]^n x K`, with `K` a `d`-simplex of volume `v`,
and let `lambda_0,...,lambda_d` be its affine barycentric coordinates.
For a binary vertex `p`, put

`q_p(z)=sum_j[(1-p_j)z_j+p_j(1-z_j)]`.

This is globally affine and equals the distance to `p` in the `l_1`
metric on the cube. Choose `0<t<1/(d+1)` and `A>1`, and take all
`2^n(d+1)` caps

`lambda_j(x)-t-A q_p(z)>=0`.                                   (5)

On the integer fibers, each cap meets only fiber `p`; its mass there is
`v(1-t)^d`. The caps strictly cover every fiber because
`max_j lambda_j(x)>=1/(d+1)>t`. For any
`tau>2^(-n) gamma_d`, one can choose `t<1/(d+1)` sufficiently close to
`1/(d+1)` that all these cap masses are strictly below `tau M`.

If the FULL ambient normal is normalized to unit length, the corresponding
hinge contribution is

`v(1-t)^(d+1) / [(d+1) sqrt(n A^2+|grad lambda_j|^2)]`.

This uses the exact tail integral
`integral_K(lambda_j-t)_+ dx=v(1-t)^(d+1)/(d+1)`.
The total potential tends to zero as `A` tends to infinity, although
every cap budget stays fixed and every fiber remains strictly covered.
The limiting normalized caps are vertical support caps and their closed
masses jump to `v`, including their entire boundary fiber.

Continuous normalization instead divides (5) by `|grad lambda_j|`.
It leaves a positive constant hinge contribution independent of `A`,
as required by (4). Thus simply normalizing all ambient normals and using
ordinary parameter compactness would lose the relevant boundary mass.

An even more direct failure occurs if coverage is weakened to
`int(Q) intersect (Z^n x R^d)=empty` for a container `Q subset C`.
For a hollow cube projection, `Q=C` meets this weaker condition and every
hinge can vanish. It does not cover its boundary fibers by the open
exterior caps. Condition (1) deliberately covers the actual full fibers.

## 3. Exact whole-fiber coverage certificates

For a fixed fiber define

`F_z=min_(x in K_z) max_i L_i(z,x)`.

Then the caps cover that entire fiber if and only if `F_z>=0`.
Finite-dimensional convex minimax gives the exact identity

`F_z=max_(lambda in Delta_N) [
       sum_i lambda_i(a_i dot z-b_i)
       -h_Kz(-sum_i lambda_i u_i)]`.                            (6)

Both extrema are attained. One elementary proof is to map `K_z` into
`R^N` by `x -> (L_i(z,x))_i`, add the positive orthant, and separate this
closed convex upper set from the open box with all coordinates below
`F_z`. A separating vector can be chosen nonnegative and normalized to
sum one. Its minimum over the image is at least `F_z`; the reverse
inequality follows by evaluating any convex combination at a minimizer
of the maximum. Compactness gives the displayed extrema.

Choose an attained maximizer `lambda_z`, and write

`U_z=sum_i lambda_zi u_i`,
`C_z=sum_i lambda_zi(a_i dot z-b_i)-h_Kz(-U_z)=F_z>=0`.          (7)

At `C_z=0` there exists a genuine contact point `x_z in K_z` with

`L_i(z,x_z)<=0` for all `i`,
`lambda_zi>0 => L_i(z,x_z)=0`,
`-U_z in N_Kz(x_z)`.                                          (8)

Here `N_K(x)={v:v dot(y-x)<=0 for all y in K}`. To verify (8), take a
minimizer of `max_i L_i` and compare it with the dual minimizer in (6).
Its maximum is zero, its weighted average equals zero, and it minimizes
`U_z dot x` on `K_z`. The contact lies in the actual mixed-integer set.
The boundary normal in (8) is retained; it need not vanish.

For reference, one can choose a certificate with at most `d+1` positive
weights: at a primal-dual saddle point, all used caps have the same
value; replace their convex combination of continuous normals by a
Caratheodory representation of the same `U_z`. This preserves both the
support value and the affine weighted value. This support count is not
an improved mixed cap-budget inequality.

## 4. Actual first variations and the normalized offset stress

For any bounded parameter variation, write
`dot L_i=dot a_i dot z+dot u_i dot x-dot b_i`.
Because `u_i` is nonzero, each boundary has zero `mu`-mass. Dominated
convergence gives the exact derivative

`dot Psi=sum_i [P_i dot dot a_i+m_i dot dot u_i-c_i dot b_i]`,   (9)

where

`c_i=mu(H_i)`, `P_i=integral_(S intersect H_i) z dmu`,
`m_i=integral_(S intersect H_i) x dmu`.

Thus the hinge gradient contains actual cap masses and first moments,
not Euclidean areas of a lattice-free container.

First choose a minimizing representative in which every threshold is
at most `B_i=max_(S)(a_i dot z+u_i dot x)`: replacing `b_i>B_i` by `B_i`
leaves its hinge and cap mass zero and can only enlarge the cap, so it
preserves coverage. Rechoose the attained fiber certificates (7) for
this representative. Fix its normals `a_i,u_i`. Let `q_i` be the least
threshold at which cap `i` has mass at most `tau M`. The cap-mass function
is continuous, nonincreasing, and ranges from `M` to zero, so `q_i`
exists, `mu(H_i(q_i))=tau M`, and the budget constraint is precisely
`b_i>=q_i`. Its upper endpoint is `B_i`, where the cap has zero mass.
One has `q_i<B_i` since `tau>0` and the fibers have interior.

Keep the certificates `lambda_z` in (7) fixed. Their coverage inequalities
are linear in `b` and still suffice for full-fiber coverage. The original
minimum is consequently a minimum of a differentiable convex function
on the compact polyhedron defined by these inequalities and the threshold
box. The polyhedral normal-cone identity (equivalently finite Farkas)
therefore gives nonnegative multipliers `eta_z,kappa_i,omega_i` with

`c_i=sum_z eta_z lambda_zi-kappa_i+omega_i`,                    (10)

`eta_z C_z=0`, `kappa_i(b_i-q_i)=0`, `omega_i(B_i-b_i)=0`.

No constraint qualification is needed for this fixed-normal statement:
the objective is differentiable convex and all constraints are linear.
If `b_i=B_i`, then `c_i=0` and `kappa_i=0`, so (10) forces
`omega_i=0` and `eta_z lambda_zi=0` for every `z`. Thus all upper
multipliers vanish, and the exact normalized stress is

`c_i+kappa_i=sum_z eta_z lambda_zi`.                           (11)

In particular

`sum_i c_i+sum_i kappa_i=sum_z eta_z`,
`kappa_i>0 => c_i=tau M`,
`sum_i(c_i+kappa_i)u_i=sum_z eta_z U_z`.                        (12)

The last right-hand side consists of the actual supporting-fiber forces
from (8), with its sign as displayed. It cannot be set to zero merely
because the global set is convex. Since the caps cover `S`, the first
identity also gives `sum_z eta_z>=sum_i c_i>=M`; this elementary mass
consequence alone does not improve the Helly constant.

At `eta_z>0`, choose the contact from (8). Equations (11)--(12) then join
cap masses from different fibers to one finite family of actual
mixed-integer contacts. They do not assert a per-group `gamma_d` bound.

## 5. Joint normals and cap budgets: an exact Fritz--John system

The same attained family is a local minimum in the joint variables
`(a_i,u_i,b_i,lambda_z)`, with `|u_i|=1`, `lambda_z in Delta_N`,
cap budgets, and the sufficient cover inequalities `C_z>=0` in (7).
The certificates are now variables as well, starting at their attained
maximizers in (6). This enlarged formulation remains feasible only when
the actual caps cover every fiber; conversely our attained solution
belongs to it, so it is a local minimum in this formulation.

For each cap there is a compact convex set of consistent generalized
cap-mass gradients

`(P_i^s,m_i^s,-S_i)`                                           (13)

in the variables `(a_i,u_i,b_i)`. It is the convex hull of limits of
ordinary gradients at nearby differentiability points of the cap-mass
function. The cap-mass function is locally Lipschitz where `u_i!=0`:
on bounded fibers a parameter change of size `epsilon` changes a cap
only inside a slab of thickness `O(epsilon)`, and every such slab has
volume at most its thickness times a fixed bound on projected area.

The entries in (13) have the following actual section interpretation.
Put

`T_iz=K_z intersect {u_i dot x+a_i dot z=b_i}`.

There are consistent measurable densities `0<=theta_iz<=1` on these
sections such that

`S_i=sum_z integral_(T_iz) theta_iz dH_(d-1)`,
`P_i^s=sum_z z integral_(T_iz) theta_iz dH_(d-1)`,
`m_i^s=sum_z integral_(T_iz) x theta_iz dH_(d-1)`.                (14)

For a proper interior section the density is one; at a supporting
facet it can vary across the facet. The same density is used in all
three entries, and it arises from the common parameter-gradient limit;
arbitrary independent choices are not asserted to be realizable.
To verify (14), project nearby sections onto the limiting cap plane.
Their Jacobians tend to one; their projected indicator densities lie
between zero and one. Compact weak limits of these bounded measures
are dominated by section Hausdorff measure and supported on `T_iz`.
At relative interior points of a proper interior section the nearby
indicators converge to one. Convex combinations of gradient limits
retain the same mass and first-moment representation. This includes
`d=1`, where a supporting section is one point and its density is a
number in `[0,1]`. A nonfacet supporting section of zero
`H_(d-1)` measure contributes zero.

There exist nonnegative numbers

`alpha_0, r_i, eta_z`, not all zero,

and consistent section data (13)--(14), such that

`r_i>0 => mu(H_i)=tau M`, `eta_z>0 => C_z=0`,

`alpha_0 c_i+r_i S_i = sum_z eta_z lambda_zi`,                  (15)

`alpha_0 P_i+r_i P_i^s = sum_z eta_z lambda_zi z`,               (16)

`alpha_0 m_i+r_i m_i^s
       =sum_z eta_z lambda_zi x_z+alpha_0 Psi_i u_i`,            (17)

where `Psi_i=integral_S(L_i)_+dmu`. Whenever `eta_z>0`, the same
point `x_z` in all equations is a genuine primal-dual contact satisfying
all three conditions (8). In particular `(z,x_z) in S`.

Here is a finite-dimensional first-order proof, including the
normalization issue. Work in local smooth charts for each unit sphere,
and in the affine hyperplanes `sum_i lambda_zi=1`; retain the active
simplex inequalities `lambda_zi>=0`. The objective has the gradient
in (9). The cap-budget gradients range over the compact convex sets
(13). For an active cover inequality, the gradients of `-C_z` range
over its exposed face `x_z in argmin_(K_z) U_z dot x`, with the SAME
point used in every parameter component:

`partial_(a_i,u_i,b_i) C_z=lambda_zi(z,x_z,-1)`,
`partial_(lambda_zi) C_z=L_i(z,x_z)`.                           (18)

These formulas follow directly from the support-function subgradient
formula; the dependence on the exposed point is affine, so convexifying
the gradient set still amounts to one point of the same exposed face.
If a chart direction had strictly negative objective derivative and
strictly negative pairing with every allowed gradient of every active
inequality, then for small positive time it would decrease the objective
and satisfy all inequalities. The Lipschitz gradient upper estimate,
or the elementary support-function directional derivative for (18),
justifies this implication even at nonsmooth caps. It contradicts
local minimality.

The union of the finitely many compact convex gradient sets is compact.
If zero did not belong to its convex hull, strict finite-dimensional
separation would provide exactly such a decreasing direction. Hence
zero is a convex combination of these gradients. Grouping the terms
gives nonnegative objective, budget, and cover multipliers, together
with normals for the active simplex inequalities and the eliminated
sphere/affine constraints. The objective, budget, and cover multipliers
cannot all vanish: positive combinations of normals `-e_i` at zero
simplex coordinates cannot vanish in the simplex tangent space, since
at least one coordinate of each simplex point is positive. Sphere
normals alone cannot vanish in the original parameter equations either.
This proves the stated nontriviality without assuming a constraint
qualification or closure of an unbounded gradient cone.

The unrestricted `a_i,b_i` equations of this separation are exactly
(15)--(16). Before simplification, its `u_i` equation has a real sphere
multiplier `sigma_i`:

`alpha_0 m_i+r_i m_i^s-sum_z eta_z lambda_zi x_z+sigma_i u_i=0`.

The `lambda_z` equations matter. For `eta_z>0`, they say that the chosen
`lambda_z` maximizes the linear vector `(L_i(z,x_z))_i` on `Delta_N`.
Its weighted value is `C_z=0`, so all these values are nonpositive and
every positively weighted value is zero. Thus (8) holds for the actual
point selected by separation, not just for some unrelated point of the
exposed face. This is why the certificate weights were allowed to vary.

Finally take the inner product of the `u_i` equation with `u_i`, and
use (15)--(16) and the common cap-contact equalities. The section term
vanishes exactly because all its points lie on `L_i=0`, including the
consistent facet traces. The cap term is exactly `alpha_0 Psi_i`.
Therefore

`sigma_i=-alpha_0 Psi_i`,                                     (19)

which proves (17), with the displayed sign and coefficient one.

Writing `W_i=alpha_0 c_i+r_i S_i`, summing (15), and using (8) also gives

`sum_i W_i=sum_z eta_z`,
`sum_i W_i u_i+sum_z (-eta_z U_z)=0`,
`-eta_z U_z in N_Kz(x_z)` when `eta_z>0`.                       (20)

Thus these forces join different contact fibers, but the continuous
normal sum generally contains nonzero supporting-fiber terms.

This identity joins actual cap mass and first moments, actual coarea
section moments, and actual contact fibers. It retains all oblique
normals and all boundary supporting forces. If `alpha_0>0`, it may be
scaled to one; if `alpha_0=0`, the hinge displacement in (17) vanishes
and only a section stress remains. No argument here excludes that
abnormal case.

For example, a direction tangent to the sphere constraints that strictly
improves every active cap budget and every active coverage inequality
(uniformly over their consistent gradient sets, and with the usual
simplex tangent conditions) would be a sufficient constraint qualification
to rule out `alpha_0=0`. Such a direction has NOT been proved to exist
at a general minimizing cover. Fixed-measure budget decrease and coverage
strictification can conflict; the common-shrink direction from a
body-volume optimization problem cannot be imported into this problem.

## 6. What the new invariant does and does not supply

The minimum of (2) is an attained positive number at fixed cap count,
fixed fiber family, and feasible cap budget. Its compactness explicitly
handles unbounded integer tilts by exact trace saturation. Equations
(11)--(12) give normalized fixed-offset cap-mass stress; equations
(15)--(19) give the full cap/section/contact moment system, with its
possible abnormal objective multiplier visible.

A bound converting these identities into `tau>=2^(-n) gamma_d` has not
been proved. In particular, neither supporting-fiber forces nor the
abnormal multiplier may be discarded, and no per-contact `gamma_d`
allocation is asserted.
